records.title: The Missing Module
records.speaker: Cian · fellow student
records.text:
It's the first week of teaching, and the buildings are beginning to feel a little less unfamiliar. You have found your way to Central Quad, although you still have to check the signs every time you leave a room. During induction, everyone talked about the freedom of the Arts programme: different subjects, possible Majors, and the chance to discover interests you hadn't expected. That sounded exciting. It also sounded much simpler when somebody was explaining it from a stage.

You sit on a low wall and open your timetable for the third time today. Most of the modules look familiar, but one subject you ranked highly when you submitted your preferences is nowhere to be seen. You remember putting it near the top of your list. You also remember mentioning it at your first advising conversation. You assumed that meant you would be taking it.

Cian, another first-year you've met twice but already recognise across campus, drops their bag beside you. “Are you still checking that thing? Mine's packed. There's a gap on Thursday, but every other day looks different.” Cian leans closer to inspect your screen. “Wait. Didn't you say you were doing that subject?”

You explain that it isn't there. Cian frowns, then shrugs. “Maybe the system's just late. Somebody in our group chat said you can turn up to the lecture and they’ll sort it. I thought we were meant to choose everything ourselves.” You remember the adviser saying something about availability, though you can't remember the exact words. You don't want to make a fuss over nothing. On the other hand, you had hoped to explore this subject before deciding what direction to take.

Cian looks up. “So what are you going to do?”

records.title: Something Unexpected
records.speaker: Saoirse · classmate
records.text:
It's the end of an introductory session in East Quad. You had only come because it appeared in the list of subjects you could explore, and you didn't know quite what else to expect. The room was lively. The lecturer showed examples from several disciplines and invited people to argue about how they might approach the same question. You had more to say than you expected.

Outside the classroom, students spill into the bright corridor. Some seem to know precisely what they want from the degree. Others are comparing modules, swapping room numbers and discovering that their timetables barely overlap. You feel a small rush of excitement: perhaps there is more here for you than the two subjects you wrote on your application.

Saoirse, who sat beside you, catches up. “That was actually great,” she says. “I didn't think I'd like it either.” You agree, then wonder how this new interest fits with the subjects you already had in mind. If you keep adding possibilities, will you eventually have to give something up?

Saoirse asks, almost casually, “So what are you going to Major in?” You start to say the subject you'd originally imagined, then stop. For the first time, you're less certain. You say, “I don't really know yet,” and hear yourself apologising as though you have failed a test. Saoirse laughs. “Neither do I. Everyone keeps asking, though.”

You still have the rest of your first year to explore, but you're beginning to suspect that some choices might matter earlier than others. How do you respond?

records.title: Two Empty Days
records.speaker: Saoirse · classmate
records.text:
Monday morning. Your phone alarm goes off at the same time it did in school, but you have no class to travel to. Tuesday is blank as well. At first, you wonder whether the timetable has failed to load. You refresh it, close it, and open it again. Nothing changes.

Later, you meet Saoirse near the Academic Hub & Library. She is carrying a coffee and complaining about having to cross campus between two classes. You show her the empty days. “Two days off?” she says. “You're joking. Mine is packed!” She starts comparing timetables on her phone. You recognise some of the same module titles, but the pattern of classes is completely different.

You remember hearing that university modules have credits attached to them. You've seen '5 ECTS' written beside several subjects, but nobody has sat beside you and explained what that might mean for a normal week. You know there will be reading and assignments; you're just not sure how to fit them into days that don't look like school days.

A notification arrives from one of your modules: reading for next week's discussion, a small task to prepare and a reminder to check the online learning space. There's also a social event you wanted to attend this afternoon. You could use the spare time to settle into the city, take on more work shifts, or begin preparing for classes. Perhaps there's a problem with the timetable after all.

Saoirse grins. “Well, what are you doing with your two days off?”

By your second week, your phone contains more university emails than you know what to do with. One message mentions registration; another directs you to a School; a third says to ask the programme team. You have also heard someone refer to the Student Hub and somebody else tell you to contact an academic adviser. The names are beginning to blur together.

You follow signs towards Rathdown House. The older building feels very different from the new teaching spaces. Inside, several students are waiting: one needs help with a student card, another is talking about an online account, and a third is trying to explain why something on their record looks wrong. You realise you aren't the only person still finding their feet.

Niamh, a member of the student-support team in this fictional story, waves you forward. “Hi. What can I help you with?” You begin with the timetable question you've been carrying around. Halfway through explaining, you remember something else: a friend told you they were struggling to attend because of difficulties at home. You are also wondering whom you would speak to if something personal began affecting your own classes.

Niamh listens, but doesn't pretend all these issues have the same solution. “We can work out where the question belongs,” she says. “Sometimes the first useful thing is finding the right person.” You have a choice about where to begin the conversation.

records.title: The Invitation
records.speaker: Rory · society organiser
records.text:
You have a gap between classes and no particular destination. For the first time since induction, you walk towards Lower House without needing to check your timetable. There is noise from a common room, a few people playing games, and a noticeboard crowded with posters. You pause by one advertising music, film, volunteering and society events.

So far, you've recognised faces without quite knowing names. A few people seem to have settled into groups already. You tell yourself you don't really need to join anything; there is enough to figure out with the modules. But you also remember spending most of the previous evening scrolling through messages rather than talking to anyone.

Rory, a student society organiser, notices you reading the posters. “Thinking of joining something?” Rory asks. “There's no audition to come to the first meeting, if that's what you're wondering.” They point towards a gathering later in the week. A handful of students are talking nearby, and one waves as if you might already be part of the group.

You don't know if you'll have time. You're not even sure whether you have the right interests. Rory adds, “People join to try things out, too. You don't have to be good at it already.” Their tone is friendly, but you still feel awkward about walking into a room where everyone might know one another.

Rory waits while you decide whether to ask a question, leave, or raise something else that's been worrying you.

records.title: The First Assignment
records.speaker: Aoife · lecturer
records.text:
It's the second week and the excitement of starting university is giving way to something more practical: actual assignments. A notification arrives from the online learning space while you're sitting in the library. It contains a brief with a deadline, a list of learning outcomes and several instructions you think you understand — until you try to picture what the finished work is supposed to look like.

The task is shorter than you expected, but it asks you to use evidence and respond to a particular question. You scroll past the marking criteria, then back up to read them again. You are used to being told exactly what to produce. Here, you seem to be expected to make more decisions yourself.

A group chat lights up. Someone says they've already finished. Another student asks whether references are needed. A third shares a screenshot of a half-written response. You feel suddenly behind, even though the assignment was only released today. You consider copying the structure of what somebody else has done, but you don't know whether it would actually address your own brief.

Aoife, one of your lecturers, is nearby speaking with another student. She seems approachable, although also busy. You could ask her what the task requires. You could first read the criteria properly or find the library's study support. Or you could start writing and hope the expectations become clearer as you go.

You open a blank document. The cursor flashes. What is your first move?

records.text:
It's a bright afternoon in the second week. You are sitting near Central Quad when Cian appears holding two coffees and a new idea. Yesterday a visiting lecturer described a subject Cian had never considered. Now Cian wants to take it. The problem is that it isn't among the six modules on the timetable.

‘This is the whole point of Arts, isn't it?’ Cian says. ‘They told us first year is for exploring. So surely we can switch things around until we find what we like.’

You remember the welcome presentation. You heard the same message: try different areas, keep an open mind, don't rush into declaring a Major. But you also remember submitting preferences, getting an allocated set of modules, and being told to check what you were registered on. Cian has already drafted a message to the lecturer: ‘Hi, I'm joining your class tomorrow.’ You can see why Cian thinks it makes sense. University is meant to offer more freedom than school. Still, if students could simply swap each week, how would classes, capacity and progression work?
